content:
The outlook for rheumatoid arthritis is much better than it was a generation ago. With early diagnosis and modern treatment, many people reach remission or low disease activity, keep working and live full lives. RA is a long-term condition that usually needs ongoing treatment, and it does raise the risk of heart disease and some other problems, but most of these risks can be reduced.

What has changed

In the past, many people with RA developed serious joint damage and disability. Today, rheumatologists start disease-modifying medicines early and adjust them until the disease is controlled, an approach called "treat to target". Biologic and targeted medicines give further options when standard treatments are not enough.

Remission

Remission means there are few or no signs of active inflammation. Many people reach it, especially when treatment starts within the first few months of symptoms. Some people can later reduce their medicines under specialist supervision, but stopping treatment yourself often leads to a flare.

What affects the outlook

Factors linked with a better outcome include:

  • early diagnosis and treatment
  • good response to the first medicines
  • not smoking
  • staying active
  • keeping to a healthy weight

Factors that may mean more active disease include positive blood tests for rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies, many swollen joints at diagnosis and early damage on X-rays. These are reasons for close monitoring, not reasons to lose hope.

Living with flares

Even when RA is well controlled, flares can happen. They may be triggered by infections, stress or missed doses. Know who to contact, as many rheumatology teams have an advice line. Steroid injections or short courses can settle a flare while longer-term treatment is reviewed.

Heart health

RA increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes, partly because of inflammation. NICE recommends assessing cardiovascular risk in people with RA. You can lower risk by:

  • getting inflammation under control
  • not smoking
  • regular exercise
  • having blood pressure and cholesterol checked and treated

Other health issues to be aware of

  • osteoporosis, especially with long-term steroids
  • infections, more likely on some treatments. Keep vaccinations up to date.
  • lung problems, which can be linked to RA or rarely to treatment. Report a new cough or breathlessness.
  • eye dryness, sometimes from Sjögren's syndrome
  • anaemia and fatigue
  • low mood, which is common and treatable

Life expectancy

RA has been linked with a shorter life expectancy on average, mainly due to heart disease and infections. With modern treatment and attention to heart health, this gap is narrowing. Your own outlook depends on many things, so ask your team about your personal situation.

Work and everyday life

Many people with RA continue to work. Under the Equality Act 2010, employers must consider reasonable adjustments. Access to Work can help with equipment and travel costs. Occupational therapists can advise on protecting your joints and managing fatigue.

Your part in a good outcome

  • take your medicines as prescribed and attend blood tests
  • tell your team about side effects rather than stopping treatment
  • stay active and keep strong
  • report new swelling or flares early
  • look after your mental health
  • ask questions and be involved in decisions

Planning ahead

If you are thinking about pregnancy, surgery, travel or changing jobs, talk to your team in advance. Many medicines need adjusting in these situations, and planning early makes everything smoother.

Many people find the first year after diagnosis the hardest, as they adjust to the condition and find the right treatment. It often gets easier with time. Support from others with RA, through local groups or national charities, can make a real difference during this period.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
